job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Drafting Analysis: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Defects

*Based on the text as amended by the October 6 manager's amendment. Please verify against the official committee print before relying on any citation.*

## A. Definitions (Sec. 2)

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A): per-vessel threshold allows fleet splitting.** The 10,000-ton trigger applies to recovery "by a single vessel," so an operation spread across several vessels, each under 10,000 tons per year, falls outside subparagraph (A) even if total output is far higher. However, subparagraph (B) may let the Secretary close this gap (see item 6).

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "per year" is undefined.** The bill doesn't say whether this means a calendar year, fiscal year, or rolling 12 months, or how a partial first year is measured. That affects both whether the threshold is crossed and when.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A): wet vs. dry tonnage is unspecified.** Freshly recovered nodules contain substantial water, so measuring by wet or dry weight could change whether an operation crosses 10,000 tons.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "recovery" and "by a vessel" are undefined.** Nodules are collected by a seafloor collector vehicle and lifted through a riser. It's unclear whether "recovery" means collection on the seabed or lifting to the surface, and whether recovery by a collector or other non-vessel platform counts as recovery "by a vessel."

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A): depth measurement and "other mineral resources" are ambiguous.** "At depths greater than 200 meters" doesn't say whether it means water depth or depth below the seafloor. "Other mineral resources" could be read to reach sand, gravel, or phosphorite, which supports an overbreadth argument.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B): "the Secretary" is never defined.** No Secretary is designated for this function. The only Secretary named anywhere in the Act is the Secretary of State (Sec. 6), which would be an odd agency to make ecological determinations. This is a clear drafting defect.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B): open-ended delegation with criminal consequences.** The Secretary can extend the prohibition to "any activity" posing "comparable" risks, with no standard, no rulemaking or notice requirement, and no procedure. Because Sec. 5(b) attaches up to 10 years' imprisonment, this supports vagueness, fair-notice, and rule-of-lenity arguments. (Nondelegation arguments are generally weak, but they are stronger where criminal liability is involved.)

8. **Sec. 2(2): "U.S. person" is narrow.** It covers only citizens and corporations "organized under the laws of a State." It omits lawful permanent residents, non-corporate entities such as LLCs and partnerships (an LLC is not technically a corporation), and foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies.

9. **Sec. 2(2): "State" is undefined.** Without a definition including D.C. and the territories, entities organized under D.C., Puerto Rico, Guam, or other territorial law arguably are not U.S. persons.

10. **Sec. 2(3): "equipped for the recovery" is ambiguous.** It's unclear whether a vessel is "equipped" if gear is removable, stored, or installed only seasonally.

11. **Sec. 2(3) vs. Sec. 2(1)(A): the vessel concepts don't line up.** The registry covers only vessels over 5,000 gross tons, but the prohibition's threshold applies to any "single vessel" of any size. Smaller recovery vessels are subject to the ban but escape reporting, which undermines enforcement.

## B. Prohibition (Sec. 3)

12. **Sec. 3(a): "in the United States" is undefined geographically.** It's unclear whether the phrase includes the territorial sea, the EEZ, the outer continental shelf, or the territories. A non-U.S. person mining in the U.S. EEZ may not be "in the United States," which leaves a significant geographic gap.

13. **Sec. 3(a): "engage in" is undefined.** The bill doesn't say whether financing, sponsoring, chartering, directing, or supplying a mining operation counts. It also doesn't reach purchasing, importing, or processing deep-sea nodules recovered by others.

14. **Sec. 3(a): no anti-evasion clause.** There's no provision covering foreign entities owned or controlled by U.S. persons, or conduct "caused" or "facilitated" by U.S. persons. Caution: a U.S. parent that directs a subsidiary's operations could still be found to "engage in" the activity itself.

15. **Sec. 3(b): mining under an "exploration license."** Exploration licenses generally do not authorize commercial recovery, yet the exemption covers "mining conducted under" one. Holders can argue it exempts any mining they conduct, which creates a substantial grandfather loophole.

16. **Sec. 3(b): the issuing authority is unspecified.** The text doesn't limit the exemption to licenses issued under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act or by the United States. It could arguably cover sponsoring-state licenses or ISA exploration contracts, though whether an ISA contract is a "license" is itself ambiguous.

17. **Sec. 3(b): no limits on duration, renewal, transfer, scope, or area.** It's unclear whether a license renewed or amended after enactment still counts as "issued before" enactment, whether the exemption survives a transfer to a new operator, and whether it extends beyond the licensed area.

18. **Sec. 3(b) with Sec. 8: pre-enactment licensing window.** Any license issued before enactment qualifies. That creates an incentive to obtain or expand licenses before signature, and the 180-day delay in Sec. 8 lets grandfathered operators scale up before the ban bites.

19. **Sec. 3(b): commercial recovery permits are not grandfathered.** Only exploration licenses are exempt, so existing DSHMRA commercial recovery permits are not. This cuts against us, but it is useful for a reliance-interest or arbitrary-line argument.

20. **Sec. 3(c): broad environmental-assessment exemption.** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, and the exemption has no tonnage cap, permit requirement, oversight, or limit on selling recovered material. It's also purpose-based, so it's unclear how mixed-purpose activity, such as a pilot collection test, is treated.

21. **Sec. 3 generally: no relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend or repeal DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.), which still directs NOAA to issue licenses and permits. That leaves two conflicting statutory regimes with no conforming amendments.

## C. Registry (Sec. 4)

22. **Sec. 4: no enforcement mechanism.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or report carries no penalty. The reporting requirement is effectively unenforceable.

23. **Sec. 4: no jurisdictional limit, deadline, or content standard.** The text applies to "each covered vessel" worldwide, including foreign vessels with no U.S. nexus. It sets no registration deadline, gives NOAA no rulemaking authority, and doesn't specify report contents, such as tonnage, location, or depth.

## D. Penalties and Enforcement (Sec. 5)

24. **Sec. 5(a): conflict with the effective date.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but under Sec. 8 the Act takes effect 180 days later. This is internally inconsistent, though a court would likely hold that no violation can occur before the effective date.

25. **Sec. 5(a): per-day penalties for an annual threshold.** A violation of the 10,000-tons-per-year threshold occurs only once the annual total is exceeded. The bill doesn't say which days count as "days on which the violation occurs": only days after crossing the threshold, all operating days that year, or something else.

26. **Sec. 5: no enforcing agency or procedure.** No agency is authorized to assess civil penalties, provide notice and a hearing, inspect, subpoena, seize, or seek forfeiture. Nor is there a provision for court jurisdiction or venue, so the civil penalty in particular has no operational machinery.

## E. International Agreement (Sec. 6)

27. **Sec. 6: ambiguous and hortatory.** It's unclear whether the 18-month deadline applies to beginning or concluding negotiations, and there's no consequence for failure. The prohibition is not contingent on other nations agreeing, which supports a unilateral-disadvantage policy argument (a policy point rather than a legal defect).

## F. Duration and Effective Date (Secs. 7–8)

28. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b): conflicting termination provisions.** Sec. 7(a) says the prohibition "shall remain in effect until" a joint resolution is enacted, while Sec. 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. The likely reading is "whichever comes first," but the text doesn't say so.

29. **Sec. 7(a): circular and legally superfluous.** Nothing directs or funds the National Academies to produce the report. A joint resolution is ordinary legislation that Congress could pass anyway. "Serious harm" is undefined.

30. **Sec. 7(b): no savings clause.** The bill doesn't say whether pending enforcement actions survive the sunset. The general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) likely applies, but how it applies to expiring statutes, as opposed to repealed ones, is not fully settled.

31. **Sec. 7(b) with Sec. 8: shortened ban period.** The sunset runs from enactment while the prohibition starts 180 days later, so the ban lasts about 9.5 years, not 10.

32. **Sec. 8: three different reference dates.** The bill uses enactment for the grandfather cutoff, enactment for penalties, enactment for the sunset, and enactment plus 180 days for the effective date. The bill would be cleaner if it stated which date governs each provision.

## Notes for the Legal Team

- **Strongest items:** 6, 7, 12, 15–17, 20, 22, and 26 are textually clear defects or significant gaps. Items 1, 8, and 14 are real but exposed to the Sec. 2(1)(B) catch-all and to "engage in" being read broadly.
- **Weak argument I left off the list:** a Fifth Amendment takings claim based on existing licenses. Courts generally don't treat government licenses and permits as compensable property.
- **Strategic trade-off:** Items you raise as making the bill "unworkable" at markup can be fixed by amendment, and fixing many of them (items 1, 8, 12, 14–17, 20) would close the gaps that help us operate. You may want to separate the defects you raise publicly from the gaps you preserve as operating room.
- **Compliance caution:** Structuring around the bill (fleet splitting, foreign subsidiaries, relying on Sec. 3(c)) carries enforcement and criminal risk given the "willfully" standard and the Secretary's discretion under 2(1)(B). Counsel should vet any such structure before relying on it.
